bib.title: Statistical Rethinking, Chapter 2: Small Worlds and Large Worlds
bib.venue: book chapter (Statistical Rethinking, CRC Press; edition not printed in the chapter text; uses R package rethinking and the map function, so the 1st edition)

question: How does a Bayesian model learn from data, built up from counting possibilities to likelihood, parameters, prior and posterior, and how is the posterior computed?
contributions: Derives Bayesian updating as counting paths through a garden of forking data (marble bag example)
Defines the components of a Bayesian model (likelihood, parameters, prior, posterior) on the globe-tossing example
Introduces three conditioning engines: grid approximation, quadratic approximation, MCMC

results.claim: A bag of 4 marbles, 3 draws with replacement, gives 4^3 = 64 possible paths per conjecture.
results.setup: Marble bag with 4 marbles (blue/white), 3 draws with replacement, conjecture of one blue and three white (Fig 2.2)
results.quote: There are 43 = 64 possible paths in total.
results.note: Exponent is lost in extraction (printed 4 cubed).

results.claim: For the observed draw sequence (blue, white, blue), ways to produce the data across the five conjectures are 0, 3, 8, 9, 0, found by multiplying per-draw counts.
results.setup: Conjecture with one blue and three white marbles; data is three draws; the 8 and 9 apply to two-blue and three-blue conjectures
results.quote: For one blue and three white, there are three ways, as we counted already. For
results.note: Table cells for 0 x 4 x 0 = 0, 1 x 3 x 1 = 3, 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, 3 x 1 x 3 = 9, 4 x 0 x 4 = 0 are on book p23.

results.claim: Updating by multiplying old counts by new counts equals recomputing from scratch when observations are independent; 8 ways times 2 ways gives 16.
results.setup: Two-blue-two-white conjecture, prior counts (0,3,8,9,0), new draw of a blue marble
results.quote: So there are 8 × 2 = 16 ways for the

results.claim: After a factory prior (blue marbles rare: 3,2,1 bags for the three middle conjectures), the two-blue conjecture is most plausible with count 32, barely above 27.
results.setup: Counts (3,16,27) multiplied by factory counts (3,2,1); prior information of a different type than the draws

results.claim: Counting sequences is impractical: ten data points already give over one million possible sequences, which is why counts are standardized to probabilities.
results.setup: Marble example with 4 outcomes per draw
results.quote: there are already more than one million possible sequences.

results.claim: Standardizing the counts (0,3,8,9,0) gives plausibilities 0.00, 0.15, 0.40, 0.45, 0.00 (R code 2.1).
results.setup: ways/sum(ways) with a flat prior over the five conjectures

results.claim: The binomial likelihood of 6 water in 9 tosses at p = 0.5 is 0.1640625.
results.setup: dbinom(6, size=9, prob=0.5), globe tossing data W L W W W L W L W

results.claim: Grid approximation of the globe posterior is already quite good at 20 points and changes little after the first 100; 5 points is terrible.
results.setup: Globe tossing, 6 W in 9 tosses, uniform prior, p_grid = seq(0,1,length.out=20); Fig 2.7 compares 5 and 20 points
results.note: Figure 2.7 caption: 5 points terrible, 20 points quite good.

results.claim: Grid size explodes with parameters: two parameters on 100 values each need 10000 evaluations, and 10 parameters need many billions.
results.note: Printed as 1002 = 10000 (100 squared) in the extracted text.

results.claim: The quadratic approximation of the globe posterior has mode 0.67 and standard deviation 0.16, with 89% interval 0.42 to 0.92.
results.setup: rethinking::map with binomial likelihood and uniform prior; compared with exact Beta(w+1, n-w+1)
results.quote: at 0.67, and its standard deviation is 0.16.

results.claim: The quadratic approximation is poor at n=9 (positive mass at p=1 although land was seen), better at n=18, nearly exact at n=36 with the same fraction of water.
results.setup: Globe tossing, uniform prior, Fig 2.8; judged by eye, no numeric error given
results.note: McElreath adds that in some model types it can remain terrible even with thousands of samples.

results.claim: Bayesian estimates have a valid interpretation at any sample size; the rule of 30 observations is called a superstition, but the price is dependence on the prior.

limits: Chapter is deliberately small-world: model logic is verified, large-world performance must be demonstrated, not deduced (book p19-20, p31).
A confident posterior does not mean a good model; estimates are conditional on the model (book p31).
Grid approximation scales poorly with parameters; quadratic approximation needs large samples or near-Gaussian posteriors; MCMC is only introduced, with details deferred to Chapter 8.
Model checking is left to the next chapter; no concrete procedure is given here.
No datasets are real; globe tossing and marble bag are toy examples. Code uses the old rethinking map function, since replaced by quap in later editions (not stated in this chapter).
practices: Design a Bayesian model with a three-step loop: data story, update, evaluate (book p28).
Write the data story as a sampling process and use it to derive the likelihood; the story is eventually discardable because many stories map to one model (book p28-29).
Treat the prior as an engineering assumption and test sensitivity by trying several priors (book p35).
Prefer weakly informative or regularizing priors over flat priors, which are rarely best (book p35).
Do not test whether model assumptions are true; check adequacy for a purpose using aspects of the data the model ignores, such as order (book p31-32).
Treat the fitting method as part of the model, since different engines can give different answers (book p39).
Grid recipe: define grid, compute prior, compute likelihood, multiply, standardize by dividing by the sum (book p39-40).
Use more grid points for more accuracy; 20 is decent and little changes after 100 for one parameter (book p40).
Use quadratic approximation: find the posterior mode, then estimate curvature (Hessian) there (book p41-42).

terms.definition: The self-contained logical world of the model, in which all possibilities are nominated.
The broader context in which one deploys a model, where there may be events not imagined in the small world.
One of the possibilities consistent with what we know, such as a bag composition.
A conjectured proportion of blue marbles, p, is usually called a parameter value; a way of indexing possible explanations of the data.
The relative number of ways that a value p can produce the data, derived by enumerating possible data sequences and eliminating those inconsistent with the data.
The prior plausibility of any specific p.
The new, updated plausibility of any specific p; the relative plausibility of parameter values conditional on the data, Pr(p|n, w).
Starting from prior plausibilities and updating them in light of data to produce posterior plausibilities; a kind of learning.
Pr(w), the likelihood averaged over the prior, which standardizes the posterior; also called evidence, probability of the data or marginal likelihood.
When there is no reason to say one conjecture is more plausible than another, weigh all conjectures equally.
Priors that gently nudge the machine and are conservative; equivalent to penalized likelihood in non-Bayesian procedures.
Approximating a continuous posterior using only a finite grid of parameter values.
Approximating the posterior near its peak by a Gaussian, i.e. representing the log-posterior with a parabola.
Maximum a posteriori, the mode of the posterior distribution.
Markov chain Monte Carlo, a family of conditioning engines that draw samples from the posterior instead of computing it directly.
A square matrix of second derivatives, here of the log posterior with respect to the parameters, used to compute the standard deviation of a quadratic approximation.

lineage.work: Borges, The Garden of Forking Paths
lineage.note: Analogy for enumerating alternative data sequences
Quoted in exercise 2E4 on the meaning of probability
Posterior = likelihood x prior / average likelihood, derived via joint probability

figures.caption: Illustration of Martin Behaim's 1492 globe, showing the small world that Colombo anticipated.
figures.why: Anchors the small world versus large world distinction.

figures.caption: The 64 possible paths generated by assuming the bag contains one blue and three white marbles.
figures.why: Shows the garden of forking data as a tree of paths.

figures.caption: After eliminating paths inconsistent with the observed sequence, only 3 of the 64 paths remain.
figures.why: Shows pruning of paths, which is what the likelihood counts.

figures.caption: The garden of forking data, showing for each possible composition of the bag the forking paths that are logically compatible with the data.

How a Bayesian model learns. Each toss of the globe produces an observation of water (W) or land (L). Previous plausibilities (dashed curve) are updated in light of the latest observation to produce a new set of plausibilities (solid curve).
figures.why: Nine panels show sequential updating from a flat prior; the curve narrows and moves with each W or L.

figures.caption: The posterior distribution, as a product of the prior distribution and likelihood. Top row: flat prior. Middle row: step prior, zero below 0.5. Bottom row: peaked prior.
figures.why: Shows how the same likelihood gives different posteriors under different priors.

figures.caption: Computing posterior distribution by grid approximation. With only 5 points (left), the approximation is terrible. But with 20 points (right), the approximation is already quite good.
Accuracy of the quadratic approximation. Exact posterior in blue, quadratic approximation black. n = 9 (w = 6), n = 18 (w = 12), n = 36 (w = 24).
figures.why: Shows the quadratic approximation converging to the exact posterior as data grows.

code.snippet:
p_grid <- seq( from=0 , to=1 , length.out=20 )
prior <- rep( 1 , 20 )
likelihood <- dbinom( 6 , size=9 , prob=p_grid )
unstd.posterior <- likelihood * prior
posterior <- unstd.posterior / sum(unstd.posterior)

prior <- ifelse( p_grid < 0.5 , 0 , 1 )
prior <- exp( -5*abs( p_grid - 0.5 ) )

globe.qa <- map(
 alist(
 w ~ dbinom(9,p) ,
 p ~ dunif(0,1)
 ) ,
 data=list(w=6) )
precis( globe.qa )

curve( dbeta( x , w+1 , n-w+1 ) , from=0 , to=1 )
curve( dnorm( x , 0.67 , 0.16 ) , lty=2 , add=TRUE )
